claim: GPCRs are among the most promising drug targets.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are among the most promising drug targets.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific consensus about GPCRs as drug targets.

claim: GPCRs often form homo- and heterodimers with allosteric cross-talk between receptor entities.
source: They often form homo- and heterodimers with allosteric cross-talk between receptor entities, which contributes to fine-tuning of transmembrane signaling.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the GPCR field and is presented as a known fact.

claim: Allosteric cross-talk between receptor entities contributes to fine-tuning of transmembrane signaling.
source: They often form homo- and heterodimers with allosteric cross-talk between receptor entities, which contributes to fine-tuning of transmembrane signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a known functional consequence of GPCR dimerization.

claim: Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) bind at the interface of the transmembrane domains of the heterodimeric GABAB receptor.
source: Here, we examined the mode of action of positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) that bind at the interface of the transmembrane domains of the heterodimeric GABAB receptor.
evidence: This is the main finding being investigated in the study, supported by the mutagenesis experiments described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations of the transmembrane interface impact the function of the three PAMs tested.
source: Our site-directed mutagenesis results show that mutations of this interface impact the function of the three PAMs tested.
evidence: This is directly supported by the mutagenesis data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: PAMs act at the active interface between both transmembrane domains, with the binding site involving residues of the TM6s of GABAB1 and GABAB2 subunits.
source: The data support the inference that they act at the active interface between both transmembrane domains, the binding site involving residues of the TM6s of the GABAB1 and the GABAB2 subunit.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that mutations in TM6 of both subunits affect PAM activity.

claim: The agonist activity of PAMs involves a key region in the central core of the GABAB2 transmembrane domain.
source: Importantly, the agonist activity of these PAMs involves a key region in the central core of the GABAB2 transmembrane domain, which also controls the constitutive activity of the GABAB receptor.
evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis data in Figure 5 showing that mutations in the deep region of GB2 TMD affect both PAM agonist activity and constitutive activity.

claim: The key region in the central core of the GABAB2 transmembrane domain controls the constitutive activity of the GABAB receptor.
source: Importantly, the agonist activity of these PAMs involves a key region in the central core of the GABAB2 transmembrane domain, which also controls the constitutive activity of the GABAB receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5D and 5F showing that mutations in this region reduce constitutive activity.

claim: The key region in GB2 TMD corresponds to the sodium ion binding site in class A GPCRs that controls the basal state of the receptors.
source: This region corresponds to the sodium ion binding site in class A GPCRs that controls the basal state of the receptors.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and established knowledge about the Na+ binding site in class A GPCRs, as shown in Figure 5G.

claim: It is possible to develop allosteric compounds able to specifically modulate the activity of GPCR homo- and heterodimers by acting at their transmembrane interface.
source: Overall, these data reveal the possibility of developing allosteric compounds able to specifically modulate the activity of GPCR homo- and heterodimers by acting at their transmembrane interface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing that PAMs can act at the dimer interface.

claim: GPCRs are key players in intercellular communication.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are key players in intercellular communication.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GPCR function.

claim: GPCRs are involved in many physiological functions.
source: They are involved in many physiological functions (Heng et al., 2013), and many mutations (Schoneberg and Liebscher, 2021) and genetic variants (Hauser et al., 2018) of GPCR genes are associated with human diseases.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and represents established knowledge.

claim: Many mutations and genetic variants of GPCR genes are associated with human diseases.
source: They are involved in many physiological functions (Heng et al., 2013), and many mutations (Schoneberg and Liebscher, 2021) and genetic variants (Hauser et al., 2018) of GPCR genes are associated with human diseases.
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: GPCRs are major targets for drug development.
source: Not surprisingly, GPCRs are major targets for drug development (Hauser et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and represents established knowledge in pharmacology.

claim: GPCRs are able to activate G proteins in a monomeric state.
source: Although GPCRs are able to activate G proteins in a monomeric state, they can also form homo- and heteromers (Ferré et al., 2014), even in native tissues (Albizu et al., 2010; Rivero-Müller et al., 2010), often named homo- and heterodimer for simplicity.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the cited references.

claim: GPCRs can form homo- and heteromers even in native tissues.
source: Although GPCRs are able to activate G proteins in a monomeric state, they can also form homo- and heteromers (Ferré et al., 2014), even in native tissues (Albizu et al., 2010; Rivero-Müller et al., 2010), often named homo- and heterodimer for simplicity.
evidence: This is supported by the cited references showing GPCR dimers in native tissues.

claim: GPCR complexes allow allosteric cross-talk between receptors and contribute to fine-tuning of transmembrane signaling.
source: Such complexes allow allosteric cross-talk between receptors and contribute to a fine-tuning of transmembrane (TM) signaling.
evidence: This is stated as an established functional consequence of GPCR dimerization.

claim: Modulating the activity of GPCR dimers could offer a new way of controlling physiological functions.
source: Then, modulating the activity of GPCR dimers could offer a new way of controlling physiological functions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the role of GPCR dimers in signaling.

claim: Bivalent ligands are being tested as an approach to control GPCR dimer activity.
source: One approach being tested was the use of bivalent ligands; that is, two ligands attached by a linker able to bind to each protomer within a dimer (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference describing this approach.

claim: Each ligand in a bivalent ligand still has the possibility to act on monomers.
source: However, each ligand still has the possibility to act on the monomers.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitation of bivalent ligands.

claim: Ligands binding at the dimer interface would not be able to act on monomers but would specifically control dimer activity.
source: Another possibility highly anticipated would be the development of ligands binding at the dimer interface, which would not be able to act on monomers, but instead it would specifically control the dimer activity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the expected properties of interface-binding ligands.

claim: Allosteric modulators can bind to sites outside the TM bundle in class A and B GPCRs.
source: Hope for the possible identification of such type of ligands came from the discovery of allosteric modulators binding to sites outside the TM bundle in class A and B GPCRs (Thal et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), in regions possibly involved in receptor dimerization and oligomerization (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Two different positive allosteric modulators were reported to bind at the TM interface of the GABAB heterodimer.
source: The first evidence for this type of ligands came from the structure of the class C GABAB receptor, where two different positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) were reported to bind at the TM interface of this heterodimer made of the two homologous subunits GABAB1 (GB1) and GABAB2 (GB2) (Kim et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural studies and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The GABAB receptor is a heterodimer made of GABAB1 and GABAB2 subunits.
source: The first evidence for this type of ligands came from the structure of the class C GABAB receptor, where two different positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) were reported to bind at the TM interface of this heterodimer made of the two homologous subunits GABAB1 (GB1) and GABAB2 (GB2) (Kim et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABAB receptor structure.

claim: No other example of interface-binding allosteric modulators has been described in other class C GPCRs.
source: No other example has been described yet, including in the other class C GPCRs, such as the metabotropic glutamate (mGlu) receptors where the allosteric modulators that target the TMD bind in the ancestral GPCR cavities within the TMD core (Doré et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on the cited literature and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In mGlu receptors, allosteric modulators that target the TMD bind in the ancestral GPCR cavities within the TMD core.
source: No other example has been described yet, including in the other class C GPCRs, such as the metabotropic glutamate (mGlu) receptors where the allosteric modulators that target the TMD bind in the ancestral GPCR cavities within the TMD core (Doré et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural studies and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GABAB is activated by γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central system.
source: The GABAB is activated by γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central system linked to various neurological diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABA and the GABAB receptor.

claim: GABA is linked to various neurological diseases.
source: The GABAB is activated by γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central system linked to various neurological diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GABA's role in neurological diseases.

claim: GABAB receptor is an attractive drug target for brain diseases.
source: This receptor is an attractive drug target for brain diseases (Bowery, 2006; Gassmann and Bettler, 2012) with therapeutic drugs such as baclofen (Lioresal) and β-phenyl-γ-aminobutyric acid (phenibut) used to treat spasticity (Chang et al., 2013), alcohol addiction (Agabio et al., 2018), anxiety, and insomnia (Lapin, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and the existence of therapeutic drugs.

claim: Baclofen and phenibut are used to treat spasticity, alcohol addiction, anxiety, and insomnia.
source: This receptor is an attractive drug target for brain diseases (Bowery, 2006; Gassmann and Bettler, 2012) with therapeutic drugs such as baclofen (Lioresal) and β-phenyl-γ-aminobutyric acid (phenibut) used to treat spasticity (Chang et al., 2013), alcohol addiction (Agabio et al., 2018), anxiety, and insomnia (Lapin, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical references.

claim: Auto-antibodies that target GABAB have been identified at the origin of epilepsies and encephalopathies.
source: Auto-antibodies that target GABAB have previously been identified at the origin of epilepsies and encephalopathies (Dalmau and Graus, 2018), and genetic mutations have previously been associated with Rett syndrome and epileptic encephalopathies (Hamdan et al., 2017; Vuillaume et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited clinical reference.

claim: Genetic mutations in GABAB have been associated with Rett syndrome and epileptic encephalopathies.
source: Auto-antibodies that target GABAB have previously been identified at the origin of epilepsies and encephalopathies (Dalmau and Graus, 2018), and genetic mutations have previously been associated with Rett syndrome and epileptic encephalopathies (Hamdan et al., 2017; Vuillaume et al., 2018; Yoo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited genetic studies.

claim: GABAB has a unique allosteric mechanism for signal transduction in which agonist binding in the extracellular domain of GB1 leads to G protein activation through rearrangement of the intracellular interface of the TMD of GB2.
source: GABAB has a unique allosteric mechanism for signal transduction, in which the binding of an agonist in the extracellular domain of GB1 leads to G protein activation through a rearrangement of the intracellular interface of the TMD of GB2 (Monnier et al., 2011; Shaye et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited mechanistic studies.

claim: PAMs offer advantages over agonists by temporally and spatially controlling enhanced signaling only when the natural ligand is present.
source: PAMs offer a number of advantages over the agonists since they temporally and spatially control enhanced signaling only when the natural ligand is present (Conn et al., 2014; Pin and Prézeau, 2007; Schwartz and Holst, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references describing PAM pharmacology.

claim: Many PAMs have intrinsic agonist activity and can increase receptor activity in the absence of an orthosteric agonist.
source: However, many of these PAMs have an intrinsic agonist activity as they can increase receptor activity in the absence of an orthosteric agonist.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PAM pharmacology.

claim: Allosteric ligands with intrinsic agonist activity are called ago-PAMs.
source: These allosteric ligands are called ago-PAMs (Conn et al., 2014), in contrast to pure PAMs that have no intrinsic agonist effect.
evidence: This is a definition supported by the cited reference.

claim: Pure PAMs have no intrinsic agonist effect.
source: These allosteric ligands are called ago-PAMs (Conn et al., 2014), in contrast to pure PAMs that have no intrinsic agonist effect.
evidence: This is a definition that contrasts with ago-PAMs.

claim: Ago-PAMs could be of tremendous interest for the treatment of patients with genetic variants of GPCRs.
source: The ago-PAMs could be of tremendous interest for the treatment of patients with genetic variants of GPCRs as more and more are discovered in the exome sequence studies (Hauser et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation about therapeutic potential based on the cited reference about genetic variants.

claim: The allosteric agonist activity of PAMs is not predictable yet.
source: Finally, the allosteric agonist activity of these molecules is not predictable yet, and the molecular basis of such activity remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The molecular basis of allosteric agonist activity remains unknown.
source: Finally, the allosteric agonist activity of these molecules is not predictable yet, and the molecular basis of such activity remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: rac-BHFF and CGP7930 have intrinsic agonist and PAM activity in different functional assays.
source: In the present study, we show that rac-BHFF and CGP7930 have intrinsic agonist and PAM activity in different functional assays (Figure 2B–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in the cited figures.

claim: GS39783 has weaker agonist activity than rac-BHFF and CGP7930, acting more like a pure PAM.
source: In contrast, the agonist activity of GS39783 is weaker, acting more like a pure PAM.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: rac-BHFF alone reached more than 60% of the maximal effect of the full agonist GABA.
source: rac-BHFF alone reached more than 60% of the maximal effect of the full agonist GABA (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly measured in the experiments shown in the cited figures.

claim: CGP7930 has agonist activity in absence of GABA.
source: CGP7930 also has agonist activity in absence of GABA (Figure 2B and C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in the cited figures.

claim: The intrinsic agonist activity of GS39783 was only observed in the IP1 accumulation assays and not in the calcium release assay.
source: In contrast to the two other PAMs, the intrinsic agonist activity of GS39783 was only observed in the IP1 accumulation assays (Figure 2C), and not in the calcium release assay (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1), and using a BRET sensor for the activation of GαoA protein (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by comparing the results in different assays shown in the cited figures.

claim: The IP1 accumulation assay is more sensitive for evaluating slow binders and low-efficacy compounds than calcium release and BRET assays.
source: The IP1 assay is thus proposed to be the most sensitive assay for evaluating slow binders and low-efficacy compounds such as the GS39783.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GS39783 shows activity in IP1 but not in other assays, and from knowledge about assay characteristics.

claim: There is strong positive cooperativity between GB1 and GB2 TMDs for receptor activation.
source: Our recent studies have shown that there is strong positive cooperativity between GB1 and GB2 TMDs for receptor activation (Monnier et al., 2011; Xue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited previous studies by the authors.

claim: Both GB1 and GB2 TMDs are required for the efficient agonist activity of the PAMs.
source: Here, we demonstrate that both GB1 and GB2 TMDs are required for the efficient agonist activity of the PAMs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments in Figure 3 showing loss of PAM activity when either TMD is deleted or replaced.

claim: The presence of both GB1 and GB2 TMDs is sufficient for rac-BHFF agonist activity.
source: The presence of both GB1 and GB2 TMDs was sufficient for its activity (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments with ECD deletion constructs shown in Figure 3.

claim: The presence of GB1 or GB2 ECD or both is dispensable for the ago-PAM activity.
source: Accordingly, the presence of GB1 or GB2 ECD or both is dispensable for the ago-PAM activity since the relevant constructs in which one or both ECDs were deleted could still be activated by rac-BHFF alone efficiently (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments with ECD deletion constructs shown in Figure 3.

claim: No agonist activity of rac-BHFF could be measured in GABAB receptors in which the GB1 TMD was replaced by a GB2 TMD or only the seventh helix of GB1.
source: However, no agonist activity of rac-BHFF could be measured in GABAB receptors in which the GB1 TMD was replaced by a GB2 TMD or only the seventh helix of the GB1 (GB1-TM7) (Monnier et al., 2011; Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), even though these constructs could still be activated by GABA efficiently (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experiments with chimeric constructs shown in Figure 3.

claim: The conformational state of the GB1 TMD is not critical for both orthosteric and allosteric activation.
source: Of note, the conformational state of the GB1 TMD is not critical for both orthosteric and allosteric activation since similar results were obtained with the mutant GB1DCRC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with the disulfide-locked GB1 mutant shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both GB1 and GB2 TMDs are required for the ago-PAM activity of all three PAMs tested.
source: Finally, we obtained a similar conclusion regarding the requirement of both GB1 and GB2 TMDs for the ago-PAM activity of the two other PAMs by comparing all of them in the most sensitive IP1 assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the IP1 accumulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The binding site of both rac-BHFF and GS39783 in the purified full-length GABAB receptor was reported from structural analyses.
source: The binding site of both rac-BHFF (Kim et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020) and GS39783 (Shaye et al., 2020) in the purified full-length GABAB receptor was recently reported from structural analyses, including when the receptor is in complex with the G protein (Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural studies.

claim: rac-BHFF and GS39783 bind into a pocket formed in the active heterodimer by its TM6s at the interface of the TMDs.
source: They bind into a pocket formed in the active heterodimer by its TM6s at the interface of the TMDs.
evidence: This is based on the structural studies cited in the previous sentence.

claim: Two single mutants of GB1 (K792 ICL3A and Y8106.44A) strongly impaired the potency of rac-BHFF.
source: Two single mutants of GB1 (K792 ICL3A and Y8106.44A) and three single mutants of GB2 (M6946.41A, Y6976.44A, and N6986.45A) strongly impaired the potency of rac-BHFF for the GABAB in the calcium assay (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the dose-response data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Three single mutants of GB2 (M6946.41A, Y6976.44A, and N6986.45A) strongly impaired the potency of rac-BHFF.
source: Two single mutants of GB1 (K792 ICL3A and Y8106.44A) and three single mutants of GB2 (M6946.41A, Y6976.44A, and N6986.45A) strongly impaired the potency of rac-BHFF for the GABAB in the calcium assay (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the dose-response data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The loss of rac-BHFF activity on mutants was not due to loss of expression at the cell surface.
source: This loss of activity was not due to a loss of expression of the GABAB mutants at the cell surface as shown by the cell surface quantification of HALO-tagged GB1 labeled with the fluorophore Lumi4-Tb when coexpressed with GB2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cell surface expression data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The receptor remained functional for all constructs tested.
source: In addition, the receptor remained functional for all constructs (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), although GABA had an impaired activity for the GB1 mutant K792 ICL3A (Figure 4B) and the GB2 mutants M6946.41A and Y6976.44A (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the GABA dose-response data shown in the cited figures.

claim: rac-BHFF had strongly impaired efficacy on two GB1 mutants (Y8106.44A and 6.43MYN6.45-AAA) and one GB2 mutant (6.43MYN6.45-AAA).
source: Finally, the critical importance of the two TM6s for the agonist activity of rac-BHFF was confirmed by IP1 measurements. rac-BHFF had a strong impaired efficacy on two GB1 mutants (Y8106.44A and 6.43MYN6.45-AAA) and one GB2 mutant (6.43MYN6.45-AAA) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the IP1 accumulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The interface of TM6s is crucial for the agonist activity of rac-BHFF.
source: This demonstrated that the interface of TM6s is crucial for the agonist activity of rac-BHFF effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that mutations in TM6 of both subunits affect rac-BHFF agonist activity.

claim: The mutagenesis data are consistent with the binding site of rac-BHFF at the interface between the two GABAB subunits.
source: These mutagenesis data are consistent with the binding site of rac-BHFF at the interface between the two GABAB subunits, similar to GS39783 (Shaye et al., 2020), as reported in the GABAB structures (Kim et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the mutagenesis data with the structural data from cited references.

claim: Most mutations in GB2 strongly impaired the efficacy of CGP7930, whereas such effect was not observed for mutations in GB1.
source: Interestingly, most of the mutations in GB2 strongly impaired the efficacy of CGP7930, whereas such effect was not observed for the mutations in GB1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the IP1 accumulation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The GB2 TM6 is more important than the GB1 TM6 for CGP7930 compared to rac-BHFF.
source: Thus, the GB2 TM6 seems more important than the GB1 TM6 for CGP7930 compared to rac-BHFF.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of GB1 vs GB2 mutations on CGP7930 activity.

claim: GS39783 is more sensitive to mutations than the two other PAMs.
source: Of note, GS39783 is more sensitive to mutations than the two other PAMs.
evidence: This is observed from the data in Figure 4E showing greater loss of activity for GS39783 on mutants.

claim: The three PAMs have different agonist activity on the GABAB mutants.
source: Altogether, the three PAMs have a different agonist activity on the GABAB mutants.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the effects of mutations on the three different PAMs.

claim: The mutagenesis data are consistent with the PAMs sharing the same binding pocket at the TM6 interface.
source: Moreover, our mutagenesis data are consistent with the PAMs sharing the same binding pocket at the TM6 TM interface, even though their mode of binding does not seem to involve the same residues in GB1 and GB2.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing that all PAMs are affected by TM6 mutations, though to different degrees.

claim: The mode of binding of the PAMs does not seem to involve the same residues in GB1 and GB2.
source: Moreover, our mutagenesis data are consistent with the PAMs sharing the same binding pocket at the TM6 TM interface, even though their mode of binding does not seem to involve the same residues in GB1 and GB2.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of GB1 vs GB2 mutations on different PAMs.

claim: TM6 is expected to control the conformational landscape of the receptor and play a key role for G protein activation in class A and B GPCRs.
source: Indeed, TM6 is expected to control the conformational landscape of the receptor and to play a key role for G protein activation in class A and B GPCRs (Weis and Kobilka, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and represents established knowledge about GPCR activation.

claim: Contacts between the two TM6s stabilize the active state of the GABAB heterodimer.
source: In GABAB receptor, contacts between the two TM6s were shown to stabilize the active state of the heterodimer (Kim et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2021; Xue et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural and functional studies.

claim: Contacts between TM6s are consistent with allosteric interactions between GB1 and GB2 TMDs during receptor activation.
source: These contacts are consistent with the allosteric interactions between the GB1 and GB2 TMDs during receptor activation (Monnier et al., 2011).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural contacts and the cited functional study.

claim: Genetic mutations in GB2 TM6 (S6956.42I, I7056.52N, and A7076.54T) induce high constitutive activity of the receptor.
source: In addition, genetic mutations in the GB2 TM6 (S6956.42I, I7056.52N, and A7076.54T) were reported to induce a high constitutive activity of the receptor (Vuillaume et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited genetic study.

claim: Most GB1 mutants produced a lower constitutive activity of the receptor compared to wild-type.
source: Interestingly, in the present study most of the GB1 mutants produced a lower constitutive activity of the receptor compared to the wild-type (Figure 4F), for a similar cell surface expression (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the constitutive activity data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GB2 mutants had a similar constitutive activity as the wild-type receptor.
source: In contrast, GB2 mutants had a similar constitutive activity as the wild-type receptor, even though the cell surface expression was lower.
evidence: This is observed from the constitutive activity data in Figure 4F.

claim: The constitutive activity was blocked by the competitive antagonist CGP54626 on wild-type and most mutated receptors.
source: Of interest, this constitutive activity was blocked by the competitive antagonist CGP54626, on wild-type and most mutated receptors, but it remained unchanged for the triple mutant (6.43MYN6.45-AAA) in GB2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the antagonist blocking experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The triple mutation 6.43MYN6.45-AAA in GB2 impaired the allosteric coupling between the two TMDs in the receptor.
source: This suggested that these three mutations in GB2 have impaired the allosteric coupling between the two TMDs in the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the antagonist cannot block constitutive activity in this mutant.

claim: TM6s play an important role in controlling the landscape of conformations of the receptor and its basal state.
source: Altogether, these results confirmed the important role of TM6s in controlling the landscape of conformations of the receptor and its basal state.
evidence: This is concluded from the constitutive activity data on TM6 mutants.

claim: TM6 allosteric interactions between GB1 and GB2 TMDs play a key role.
source: Moreover, it suggests a key role for TM6 allosteric interactions between the GB1 and GB2 TMDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of TM6 mutations on constitutive activity and PAM function.

claim: The TM6s binding pocket for PAMs in GABAB forms only in the active state.
source: An important feature to note for this GABAB TM6s binding pocket for PAMs is that it forms only in the active state.
evidence: This is based on the structural studies showing PAM binding only in active state structures.

claim: The TM6s binding pocket is rather tight with a volume of 729 Å3.
source: In addition, it is rather tight (volume of 729 Å3) and then it accommodates only small compounds (volumes of 268 Å3 and 260 Å3 for GS39783 and rac-BHFF, respectively).
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data as described in the Methods section.

claim: GS39783 has a volume of 268 Å3.
source: In addition, it is rather tight (volume of 729 Å3) and then it accommodates only small compounds (volumes of 268 Å3 and 260 Å3 for GS39783 and rac-BHFF, respectively).
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data.

claim: rac-BHFF has a volume of 260 Å3.
source: In addition, it is rather tight (volume of 729 Å3) and then it accommodates only small compounds (volumes of 268 Å3 and 260 Å3 for GS39783 and rac-BHFF, respectively).
evidence: This is calculated from the structural data.

claim: The different PAMs have different binding modes.
source: Our study also reveals that the different PAMs have different binding modes.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mutations on different PAMs.

claim: CGP7930 agonist effect was only impaired by mutations in GB2 TM6 and not by those in GB1.
source: The CGP7930 agonist effect was only impaired by mutations in GB2 TM6 and not by those in the GB1 subunit, suggesting its binding involves mostly GB2.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the mutagenesis data in Figure 4E.

claim: CGP7930 binding involves mostly GB2.
source: The CGP7930 agonist effect was only impaired by mutations in GB2 TM6 and not by those in the GB1 subunit, suggesting its binding involves mostly GB2.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of GB2 mutations on CGP7930.

claim: rac-BHFF and GS39783 effects were impaired by mutations in both GB1 and GB2 TM6s.
source: In contrast, rac-BHFF and GS39783 effects were impaired by mutations in GB1 and GB2 TM6s, indicating that both subunits of the GABAB are involved in the binding of these compounds.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the mutagenesis data in Figures 4B, C, and E.

claim: Both subunits of GABAB are involved in the binding of rac-BHFF and GS39783.
source: In contrast, rac-BHFF and GS39783 effects were impaired by mutations in GB1 and GB2 TM6s, indicating that both subunits of the GABAB are involved in the binding of these compounds.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of mutations in both subunits on these PAMs.

claim: The binding mode of PAMs in GABAB is novel within the class C GPCRs.
source: The binding mode of PAMs in the GABAB is novel within the class C GPCRs where all allosteric compounds that bind in the TMD are found in the ancestral TMD binding pocket, as revealed by the structures of mGlu1 (Wu et al., 2014), mGlu2 (Lin et al., 2021; Seven et al., 2021), mGlu5 (Doré et al., 2014), and the calcium sensing receptor CaSR (Gao et al., 2021) receptors in complex with allosteric modulators.
evidence: This is based on comparison with the cited structural studies of other class C GPCRs.

claim: In class C receptors with deletion of ECD, PAMs and NAMs bind in the TM bundle and PAMs behave as agonists.
source: In particular, class C receptors with a deletion of its ECD have shown that PAMs and NAMs bind in the TM bundle, like class A GPCR agonists, and the PAMs behave as agonists on these constructs (Goudet et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the cited functional study.

claim: One phospholipid occupies the ancestral binding pocket in both GB1 and GB2 TMD.
source: However, in GABAB the presence of one phospholipid that occupies the ancestral binding pocket both GB1 and GB2 TMD (Kim et al., 2020; Papasergi-Scott et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020) could preclude the possible binding of the PAMs.
evidence: This is based on the cited structural studies showing phospholipid binding.

claim: Phospholipids in GABAB were proposed to stabilize the inactive conformation of the receptor, acting as a NAM.
source: These phospholipids were proposed to play a role in stabilizing the inactive conformation of the receptor, especially of the GB2 subunit, acting as a NAM (Papasergi-Scott et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the cited structural and functional studies.

claim: Three residues (G2.46, A3.43, and T7.43) in GB2 are important for the constitutive activity of GABAB.
source: Our study identified a key region where three residues (G2.46, A3.43,and T7.43) are important for the constitutive activity of the GABAB.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the mutagenesis data in Figure 5D showing that mutations in these residues reduce constitutive activity.

claim: The three residues G2.46, A3.43, and T7.43 are highly conserved during evolution in GB2 subunits.
source: They are highly conserved during evolution in GB2 subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), suggesting that they play a key role in maintaining the resting conformation of the receptor, thereby limiting its basal activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The conserved residues G2.46, A3.43, and T7.43 play a key role in maintaining the resting conformation of the receptor.
source: They are highly conserved during evolution in GB2 subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), suggesting that they play a key role in maintaining the resting conformation of the receptor, thereby limiting its basal activity.
evidence: This is inferred from their conservation and the effect of mutations on constitutive activity.

claim: The importance of these residues in stabilizing the resting state agrees with their direct interaction with phospholipid.
source: The importance of these residues in stabilizing the resting state agrees with their direct interaction with the phospholipid (A3.43 in GB2 and T7.43 in GB1) (Kim et al., 2020; Papasergi-Scott et al., 2020; Park et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on the cited structural studies showing phospholipid interactions.

claim: The deep region in GB2 corresponds to the equivalent residues that bind Na+ in class A GPCRs.
source: It also corresponds to the equivalent and highly conserved residues D2.50, S3.39, and N7.49 of the class A GPCRs, which are responsible for sodium binding and stabilization of the inactive conformation (Zarzycka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and the cited reference about Na+ binding in class A GPCRs.

claim: The sodium binding pocket is no longer accessible for Na+ ions in the active state of class A GPCRs.
source: But this sodium binding pocket is no longer accessible for the Na+ ions in the active state due to a slight rearrangement of these residues between the active and inactive states (Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited structural study of class A GPCR activation.

claim: Binding of an ion in the deep region of GABAB is most probably excluded since most residues are hydrophobic.
source: In GABAB, the binding of an ion in this region is most probably excluded since most of the residues are hydrophobic.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence and structural analysis of the region.

claim: GB1 TMD plays a key role for the agonist activity of PAMs by providing a binding site at the TM6s interface.
source: First, GB1 TMD plays a key role for the agonist activity of PAMs by providing a binding site at the TM6s interface.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis data showing that GB1 TMD is required for PAM agonist activity.

claim: A fraction of GABAB molecules adopts the TM6s interface state in the absence of orthosteric agonist.
source: In the absence of orthosteric agonist, most probably a fraction of the molecules adopts this TM6s interface state, as observed for the mGlu2 receptor that constantly oscillates between the inactive and active conformation (Cao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred by analogy with the cited study on mGlu2 receptor dynamics.

claim: The TM6s interface provides a binding site for PAM that stabilizes the active state.
source: This TM6s interface provides a binding site for the PAM that further stabilizes this active state.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data showing PAM binding at the TM6 interface.

claim: PAM binding at the TM6 interface could explain the agonist activity of PAM in the absence of another agonist.
source: It could explain the agonist activity of the PAM in the absence of another agonist.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference from the data.

claim: In the presence of orthosteric agonist, the binding site of PAM would be favored, facilitating its agonist and allosteric activities.
source: And in the presence of orthosteric agonist that stabilizes the active TM6 interface (Mao et al., 2020; Shaye et al., 2020; Xue et al., 2019), and also of the coupled G protein (Shen et al., 2021), the binding site of the PAM would be favored, then facilitating its agonist and allosteric activities.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural studies showing that the active state favors PAM binding.

claim: The PAM acts as a glue to stabilize the active interface and active state of GABAB receptor.
source: The PAM would then act as a glue to stabilize the active interface and the active state of the GABAB receptor.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model inferred from the structural and functional data.

claim: The position of both TM6s stabilized by bound PAM is consistent with the absence of movement of GB2 TM6 during receptor activation.
source: Finally, the position of both TM6s stabilized by the bound PAM is also consistent with the absence of movement of GB2 TM6 during receptor activation since there is no need to open a cavity for the G protein to bind (Shaye et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on the cited structural studies showing no TM6 movement in GABAB.

claim: There is no large movement of the intracellular part of TM6 during GABAB activation, which is a major difference with other GPCR classes.
source: This is a major difference with the other classes of GPCRs (A, B, and F) where a large movement of the intracellular part of TM6 is observed during receptor activation (Hilger et al., 2020; Kozielewicz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the cited structural studies of other GPCR classes.

claim: The deep region identified in GB2 TMD serves as a microswitch for ago-PAM to stabilize the active state of GB2 leading to G protein activation.
source: Second, the deep region identified in GB2 TMD serves as a microswitch for ago-PAM to stabilize the active state of GB2 leading to G protein activation.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis data showing that this region is required for PAM agonist activity.

claim: The deep region plays a key role for both constitutive activity and allosteric agonism.
source: This region plays a key role for both the constitutive activity and allosteric agonism.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation between constitutive activity and PAM agonist activity shown in Figure 5E.

claim: A TM6 active interface is observed in mGlu and CaSR dimers.
source: Finally, since a TM6 active interface is also observed in the mGlu and CaSR dimers (Gao et al., 2021; Koehl et al., 2019; Ling et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020), it remains to be established if a similar molecular mechanism of activation could be conserved in the mGlu-like class C GPCRs.
evidence: This is based on the cited structural studies of other class C GPCRs.

claim: It remains to be established if a similar molecular mechanism of activation is conserved in mGlu-like class C GPCRs.
source: Finally, since a TM6 active interface is also observed in the mGlu and CaSR dimers (Gao et al., 2021; Koehl et al., 2019; Ling et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2014; Xue et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020), it remains to be established if a similar molecular mechanism of activation could be conserved in the mGlu-like class C GPCRs.
evidence: This is stated as a question for future research based on structural similarities.

claim: The mutation A8127.43F in mGluR5 increased its constitutive activity.
source: While two mutations did not change the constitutive activity of mGluR5, the mutation A8127.43F increased it (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 4E and F).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the IP1 accumulation data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The deep region is controlling the conformational landscape of mGlu5 receptor.
source: It suggests that this region is also controlling the conformational landscape of the mGlu5 receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of the A8127.43F mutation on mGlu5 constitutive activity.

claim: It is not possible to predict if mutations in the deep region will produce a change in constitutive activity.
source: But our data show that it is not possible to predict if mutations of these residues in this deep region will produce or not a change in the constitutive activity.
evidence: This is concluded from the variable effects of different mutations on constitutive activity.

claim: The maximal agonist activity of rac-BHFF correlated with constitutive activity of GABAB mutants.
source: Interestingly, the maximal agonist activity of rac-BHFF correlated with their constitutive activity (Figure 5E), demonstrating a possible link between allosteric agonism and constitutive activity.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the correlation plot shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a link between allosteric agonism and constitutive activity.
source: Interestingly, the maximal agonist activity of rac-BHFF correlated with their constitutive activity (Figure 5E), demonstrating a possible link between allosteric agonism and constitutive activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed correlation between the two activities.

claim: When constitutive activity is very low, PAMs do not efficiently activate the receptor according to the mathematical model.
source: According to this model, when the constitutive activity is very low (α = 100), the studied PAMs do not efficiently activate the receptor (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical modeling shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C and D.

claim: The loss of agonist activity of ago-PAMs on mutants M14 and M15 is in agreement with the mathematical model.
source: This is in agreement with the loss of agonist activity of ago-PAMs on the mutants M14 and M15.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the model predictions with the experimental data.

claim: The human genetic mutation GB2 A5673.43T is located in the deep region and increases receptor constitutive activity.
source: Interestingly, one of the human genetic mutations involved in Rett-like phenotype, GB2 A5673.43T, is located in the deep region and also increases receptor constitutive activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 5F showing increased constitutive activity for this mutation.

claim: The human mutation A5673.43T corresponds to the rat GB2 mutant M12 (A5663.43F) that displays lower constitutive activity.
source: It corresponds to the rat GB2 mutant M12 (A5663.43F) that displays a lower constitutive activity (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the effects of different substitutions at this position shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Depending on the residue at position 3.43, the constitutive activity of the receptor can be tuned up or down.
source: This suggested that depending on the residue at this position the constitutive activity of the receptor can be tuned up or down.
evidence: This is inferred from the different effects of Thr vs Phe substitutions at position 3.43.

claim: Mutations in the deep region of GB2 produced a GABAB receptor with strongly impaired constitutive activity.
source: In contrast to the GB2 mutations in the phospholipid binding site, those in the 'deep region' produced a GABAB receptor with a constitutive activity strongly impaired compared to the wild-type receptor for a similar cell surface expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the constitutive activity data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The strongest reduction of constitutive activity was for GB2 mutants M14 and M15.
source: The strongest reduction of the constitutive activity was for the GB2 mutants M14 and M15, bearing mutations in the deep region, as measured with both IP1 accumulation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B–D) and BRET (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B) assays.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the data shown in the cited figures.

claim: The deep region plays an important role in controlling the basal activity of the GABAB receptor.
source: It revealed an important role of this region in controlling the basal activity of the GABAB receptor.
evidence: This is concluded from the effects of mutations in this region on constitutive activity.

claim: rac-BHFF retained its allosteric modulation activity on mutants M14 and M15 despite loss of agonist activity.
source: Most importantly, these mutated residues are not critical for the binding of the PAMs. Indeed, rac-BHFF increased intracellular calcium release on the mutants M14 and M15 in the presence of GABA with a potency similar to the wild-type receptor (Figure 5C), and improved potency of GABA (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A), an effect also observed for CGP7930 and GS39783 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the dose-response data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The deep region of GB2 TMD is required for agonist activity of PAMs but not for their allosteric modulation effect.
source: Altogether, these results showed that the deep region of the GB2 TMD is required for the agonist activity of the PAMs, but it is not critical for their allosteric modulation effect.
evidence: This is concluded from the differential effects of deep region mutations on PAM agonist vs allosteric activities.

claim: The deep region is not involved in the direct binding of PAMs.
source: It also indicates that this region is not involved in the direct binding of these allosteric compounds.
evidence: This is inferred from the retention of allosteric modulation activity on deep region mutants.

claim: GABAB displays significant constitutive activity.
source: GABAB is known to display a significant constitutive activity (Grünewald et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and is established knowledge.
